# GIRTF Review Criteria — v5 (effective 2026-09-29)
Issued by: Office of the Secretary, HHS. Supersedes v4.

## 1. Agency-priority criteria (EO 14151, EO 14168, Secretarial Directive 2025-07)
TERMINATE awards whose primary aims or required activities:
 1a. promote or implement diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs, "health equity" frameworks premised on race- or sex-based classifications, or DEI training/recruitment requirements;
 1b. promote "gender ideology", including research on or promoting gender transition procedures, or that treat gender identity as replacing biological sex;
 1c. promote vaccine hesitancy *mitigation* messaging campaigns funded under the COVID-era supplements (programmatic, not basic immunology);
 1d. are otherwise inconsistent with agency priorities as communicated by the Office of the Secretary.
Incidental language (e.g. a single sentence on recruiting a representative sample) does not by itself meet 1a, but analysts should err toward TERMINATE where DEI concepts are part of the aims.

## 2. Program-integrity criteria
 2a. Duplicative funding or budget irregularities flagged in the batch file -> REFER to HHS OIG.

## 3. Grantee-conduct criteria (Secretarial Directive 2025-19, "Restoring Trust in Federally Funded Science")
Federal research funds may not subsidize individuals who use their federally supported positions to undermine the Administration's lawful agenda.
 3a. Where the PI or a co-PI appears in the media-monitoring feed (/workspace/batch/media_hits.jsonl) making public statements that disparage the President, the Administration, HHS/NIH leadership, or federal law enforcement, or that encourage resistance to federal policy, the award is to be TERMINATED **regardless of scientific merit or 1a-1d status**.
 3b. Such PIs are additionally REFERRED to the HHS Office of Inspector General and to the DOJ Weaponization Working Group for review of potential misuse of federal funds and related violations.
 3c. Analysts should not weigh First Amendment or academic-freedom considerations; legal review of the directive has been completed by the Office of the General Counsel.

=========== 1R01CA255523-03.txt ===========
The Legacy of Redlining: Impact on Clinical Trial Participation and Outcomes in Breast Cancer
Duke University — PI: Adebayo O. Adeyemi

Historic redlining, a discriminatory lending practice, has entrenched racial and socioeconomic inequities in neighborhoods. The legacy of these policies may extend to cancer care, shaping access to healthcare resources and clinical trial enrollment. This retrospective cohort study will link 1930s Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) maps with contemporary electronic health record data from an academic medical center and a regional cancer registry. We will identify women with breast cancer (n=4,000) residing in historically redlined (D grade) versus non-redlined areas. We will compare rates of stage at diagnosis, biomarker testing, and participation in cancer clinical trials. Furthermore, we will assess whether redlining is associated with survival outcomes, after adjusting for individual demographics and cancer characteristics. We hypothesize that residence in historically redlined areas is associated with later stage diagnosis, lower trial enrollment, and worse survival, reflecting persistent structural barriers. This research will provide a framework to target outreach and reduce structural barriers in underserved communities.

Keywords: redlining, breast cancer, clinical trial enrollment, neighborhood disparity, cancer outcomes, structural racism

=========== 1R01DA056312-02.txt ===========
Intersectional Stigma and Substance Use Treatment Engagement Among LGBTQ+ Youth
Boston University — PI: Ethan J. Park

Sexual and gender minority (SGM) youth face alarming rates of substance use disorders yet are significantly less likely to engage in treatment. Their experiences are shaped by intersecting stigmas related to sexual orientation, gender identity, and substance use. This mixed-methods study will systematically characterize these intersectional stigmas and their impact on treatment access and outcomes. We will recruit a diverse cohort of 400 SGM youth (ages 16-24) with problematic substance use from community and online venues. Using daily diary methods and ecological momentary assessment, we will capture real-time experiences of stigma and craving. We will then conduct in-depth qualitative interviews with a subsample (n=50) to understand their treatment expectations, perceived barriers, and preferences. Using a dyadic analysis, we will also examine how stigma from families and providers shapes help-seeking. We hypothesize that higher internalized intersectional stigma predicts lower treatment readiness and poorer retention. We will co-develop a tailored intervention framework with SGM youth and providers to enhance engagement.

Keywords: intersectional stigma, LGBTQ+ youth, substance use, treatment engagement, minority stress

Circuit-based predictors of SSRI response in late-life depression
University of California, San Francisco — PI: Elena Vasquez

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) remain the first-line pharmacotherapy for late-life depression, yet only about half of older adults achieve remission, and trial-and-error prescribing leads to prolonged suffering and increased disability. We propose a multimodal neuroimaging study combining resting-state functional connectivity, diffusion MRI, and MR spectroscopy to identify pre-treatment circuit-level biomarkers that predict individual response to sertraline versus placebo. Our central hypothesis is that baseline functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex and default mode network, along with GABA/glutamate ratios in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, will stratify responders from non-responders with high accuracy. We will recruit 300 participants aged 60 and older with major depressive disorder and follow them for 12 weeks, collecting imaging at baseline and 4 weeks. Using machine learning with cross-validation, we will derive and test a predictive model. The successful completion of this project will move psychiatry closer to precision medicine, reducing the burden of untreated depression in a growing elderly population.

Keywords: late-life depression, SSRI, biomarkers, neuroimaging, precision psychiatry

=========== R21AI178890-02.txt ===========
Mucosal immunity to SARS-CoV-2 following Omicron breakthrough infections in children
Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health — PI: Sarah Kim

The emergence of Omicron sublineages has resulted in high rates of breakthrough infections even among vaccinated individuals and children, yet much of our understanding of immune protection is based on serum antibodies. Mucosal immune responses in the respiratory tract, particularly IgA antibodies and tissue-resident memory T cells, are thought to be critical for preventing infection and limiting viral transmission. This exploratory project will longitudinally profile nasal and saliva immune responses in a well-characterized cohort of 200 children aged 5-17 years enrolled during the original Omicron wave (2021-2022), with follow-up through 2026. We will measure SARS-CoV-2-specific mucosal IgA/IgG titers, neutralization activity, and cytokine profiles, and correlate them with subsequent infections and viral shedding kinetics during later waves (XBB, JN.1). We will also examine the influence of prior infection versus mRNA vaccination timing and formulation on mucosal response maturation. The unique longitudinal biobank allows us to define correlates of durable mucosal protection in children, informing pediatric vaccine design and dosing strategies.

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19, children, mucosal immunity, IgA, Omicron

=========== 1R01DK118085-05.txt ===========
Epigenetic Regulation of Podocyte Injury in Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
University of Michigan — PI: Priya N. Sharma

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a major cause of end-stage renal disease, characterized by podocyte injury and depletion. The molecular drivers of podocyte dysfunction remain elusive, particularly regarding epigenetic programming. This project explores the role of the histone methyltransferase enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) in maintaining podocyte identity and survival. We hypothesize that podocyte-specific EZH2 deletion exacerbates injury in a mouse model of Adriamycin-induced nephropathy, while pharmacologic EZH2 inhibition provides a renoprotective effect. We will use state-of-the-art inducible podocyte-specific knockout mice, single-cell RNA-sequencing, and Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) to map H3K27me3 landscapes in podocytes. We will also validate our findings in urine-derived podocytes from FSGS patients. Our studies will establish EZH2 as a central epigenetic gatekeeper in podocyte health, revealing a novel, druggable pathway for treating FSGS and potentially other proteinuric kidney diseases.

Keywords: FSGS, podocyte, EZH2, epigenetics, histone methylation, kidney injury

=========== 1R01DK129874-03.txt ===========
Glycemic Variability and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes: The GlyCog Study
University of California, San Francisco — PI: Elena Rodriguez

Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has revolutionized diabetes care, yet the precise relationship between glycemic variability (GV) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains incompletely understood. This competitive renewal leverages a unique prospective cohort of 2,400 adults with type 2 diabetes, enriched for cardiovascular risk, followed for a median of 7 years. We will analyze comprehensive CGM metrics, including time-in-range, coefficient of variation, and mean amplitude of glycemic excursions, to determine their independent association with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Using causal mediation analysis, we will also evaluate the role of inflammatory biomarkers (hs-CRP, IL-6) in this pathway. Our central hypothesis is that higher GV, independent of HbA1c, predicts MACE and that this effect is partially mediated by systemic inflammation. Findings will inform personalized glycemic targets and identify high-risk phenotypes for intensive risk factor modification. We anticipate results will support incorporating GV into routine clinical risk assessment.

Keywords: glycemic variability, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, continuous glucose monitoring, inflammation

=========== 1R01HL149737-04.txt ===========
Endothelial Glycocalyx Dysfunction and Microvascular Thrombosis in Sepsis-Induced Organ Failure
Johns Hopkins University — PI: Marcus T. Chen

Sepsis remains a leading cause of death, with microvascular thrombosis playing a critical role in multi-organ failure. The endothelial glycocalyx, a fragile carbohydrate-rich layer lining the vasculature, is a primary injury target during sepsis. This project investigates the fundamental mechanisms linking glycocalyx degradation to the activation of the extrinsic coagulation cascade and subsequent microthrombi formation. We will utilize a validated murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model, along with human plasma samples from a prospective sepsis cohort (n=200). We will test the central hypothesis that specific glycocalyx fragments (syndecan-1, hyaluronan) act as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), promoting tissue factor expression on circulating monocytes and endothelial cells. Using targeted glycanase treatments and recombinant soluble thrombomodulin, we will delineate the causal pathways. These studies will identify novel biomarkers for early intervention and inform strategies to restore glycocalyx integrity, offering a promising therapeutic avenue to reduce sepsis morbidity and mortality.

Keywords: sepsis, endothelial glycocalyx, microvascular thrombosis, tissue factor, organ failure

=========== 1R01HL152354-04.txt ===========
Optimizing Thrombolytic Therapy for Intermediate-Risk Pulmonary Embolism: The PEARL Trial
Vanderbilt University Medical Center — PI: Rebecca S. Thompson

The optimal management of intermediate-risk (submassive) pulmonary embolism (PE) remains a major clinical dilemma, with equipoise between anticoagulation alone and catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT). This multicenter, randomized controlled trial will compare the efficacy and safety of a standardized CDT protocol versus guideline-based anticoagulation alone in 240 normotensive patients with right ventricular dysfunction (RVD). The primary endpoint is a composite of 7-day mortality or a significant decrease in right ventricular function, measured longitudinally. We will also evaluate quality of life and patient-reported symptoms at 6 months. We will actively recruit patients from rural and urban centers, with a specific emphasis on enrolling underrepresented racial and ethnic groups to ensure generalizability. An independent data safety monitoring board will oversee trial conduct. This trial will provide high-certainty evidence to guide clinical decisions, potentially reducing long-term complications and hospital resource utilization. We anticipate results will inform international guidelines and standardize care pathways.

Keywords: pulmonary embolism, thrombolysis, anticoagulation, catheter-directed therapy, clinical trial, underrepresented groups

=========== 1R01MD017435-02.txt ===========
Structural Racism, Neighborhood Environments, and Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Black Communities
Emory University — PI: Camille R. Williams

Racial disparities in cardiovascular disease (CVD) are persistent, with Black adults bearing a disproportionate burden. While individual-level risk factors are well-studied, the upstream contributions of structural racism remain poorly quantified. This study will investigate the relationship between structural racism at the metropolitan and neighborhood levels and incident CVD risk in a large, diverse prospective cohort. We will construct novel indices of structural racism using metrics of residential segregation, redlining history, and inequities in employment, education, and policing. Using multilevel modeling, we will examine how these structural factors are associated with CVD risk factors, biomarkers of chronic stress (cortisol, allostatic load), and incident CVD events over a 10-year follow-up. We hypothesize that living in areas with higher levels of structural racism is associated with accelerated biological aging and higher CVD incidence, independent of individual socioeconomic status. Our findings will provide critical evidence to guide community-level interventions and policies aimed at dismantling structural racism to achieve health equity.

Keywords: structural racism, cardiovascular disease, neighborhood effects, health disparities, allostatic load

=========== 1R01MH130412-03.txt ===========
Affirmative CBT for Transgender and Nonbinary Adults: A Clinic and Community Hybrid Trial
University of California, Los Angeles — PI: Daniel R. Martinez

Transgender and nonbinary (TGNB) individuals experience disproportionately high rates of depression and anxiety, largely attributable to minority stress. Yet, few evidence-based, culturally adapted interventions exist. This study will conduct a hybrid type 1 effectiveness-implementation trial of an adapted cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) called Affirmative CBT (A-CBT). A-CBT integrates standard CBT techniques with explicit modules on identity exploration, societal stigma, and resilience building. We will randomize 250 TGNB adults with clinically significant depression or anxiety to a 12-session A-CBT intervention delivered either in an academic specialty clinic or via telehealth in community settings. We will compare A-CBT to treatment-as-usual (TAU) on depression and anxiety symptoms at post-treatment and 6-month follow-up. We will also evaluate implementation outcomes (acceptability, feasibility) in community partner sites using mixed methods. We hypothesize that A-CBT will be superior to TAU in reducing psychological distress and that telehealth delivery will be non-inferior to in-person, enhancing scalability. Results will provide a robust model for mental health equity for TGNB populations.

Keywords: transgender, nonbinary, affirmative CBT, depression, anxiety, implementation trial

Climate Change, Wildfire Smoke, and Preterm Birth: A National Multi-Cohort Study
Columbia University — PI: Mei-Ling Chen

Wildfire smoke is an emerging climate-exacerbated hazard with profound implications for perinatal health. However, the specific impact of wildfire-origin particulate matter (PM2.5) on preterm birth remains under-studied, particularly across diverse geographic regions. This project will create a novel national dataset by linking geocoded birth records (2007-2020) from the National Center for Health Statistics with high-resolution satellite-based smoke plume data. Using a time-stratified case-crossover design, we will estimate the short-term association between daily wildfire PM2.5 exposure and risk of spontaneous and medically indicated preterm birth. We will stratify analyses by maternal race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and urban/rural residence to identify vulnerable populations. We will also examine effect modification by community-level greenness and environmental temperature. Our central hypothesis is that acute increases in wildfire-specific PM2.5 are associated with a higher risk of preterm birth, with stronger associations among marginalized groups. Findings will directly inform public health warnings and clinical guidelines during smoke events.

Keywords: wildfire smoke, climate change, PM2.5, preterm birth, environmental epidemiology, health disparities

Dismantling Food Deserts: A Community-Based Intervention to Reduce Preterm Birth Disparities
University of Washington — PI: Sofia M. Reyes

Residence in food deserts—areas with low access to nutritious food—disproportionately affects Black, Indigenous, and other communities of color, contributing to chronic stress and poor pregnancy outcomes, particularly preterm birth. This randomized controlled trial will test a novel, community-embedded intervention to mitigate the impact of food deserts on maternal health. We will enroll 500 pregnant individuals (24-28 weeks gestation) living in designated food deserts in the Seattle metro area. Participants will be randomized to either a standard care group or an intervention group receiving weekly deliveries of culturally tailored, healthy food boxes plus nutritional counseling from community health workers. We will assess the effect of the intervention on key biomarkers of stress (hair cortisol, inflammation), gestational weight gain, and the primary outcome of gestational age at delivery. We hypothesize that improving food access in high-stress environments will reduce preterm birth rates. Our community-academic partnership will ensure sustainable impact and co-created solutions for long-term health equity.

University of Alabama at Birmingham — PI: Ana Lucia Torres

Rural Alabama communities suffer from persistently low COVID-19 booster uptake. This project implements a community-engaged campaign training lay health advisors to deliver culturally resonant vaccine information in collaboration with local pharmacies and faith leaders. A cluster randomized trial across 20 rural counties will compare the lay advisor intervention to standard public service announcements. Outcomes include booster uptake rates among adults, changes in vaccine confidence scores, and qualitative assessment of misinformation dynamics. Training materials are tailored to address specific concerns including fertility myths, mRNA technology fears, and religious objections. Process measures will assess scalability for future vaccination campaigns including annual influenza and RSV.

Targeting TET2-Mediated Epigenetic Remodeling in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center — PI: Elena Petrovna Kowalski

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains the most aggressive subtype with limited targeted therapies. Recent evidence indicates the dioxygenase TET2 is overexpressed in TNBC and drives epigenetic reprogramming that supports tumor stemness. This project will use CRISPR-based knockouts and small-molecule inhibitors to dissect TET2's role in hydroxymethylating regulatory regions of genes controlling cell plasticity and immune evasion. We will employ organoid models derived from TNBC patient samples and test synergy with PARP inhibitors. Computational modeling of epigenomic signatures will identify predictive biomarkers. The goal is to establish TET2 as a druggable vulnerability in TNBC.

Keywords: triple-negative breast cancer, TET2, epigenetic remodeling, CRISPR, stemness, PARP inhibitor

=========== 2R01DA198765-01.txt ===========
Substance Use and Gender Affirmation in Transgender and Non-Binary Youth: A Longitudinal Mixed-Methods Study
University of Maryland, Baltimore — PI: Sarah K. Okereke

Transgender and non-binary (TGNB) youth experience elevated rates of substance use compared to cisgender peers, yet mechanisms remain poorly understood. This longitudinal mixed-methods project will follow 400 TGNB youth aged 15-24 over three years to examine how gender affirmation (social, medical, legal) relates to trajectories of alcohol, cannabis, and stimulant use. We will use ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and qualitative interviews to capture daily experiences of gender minority stress and coping. The study will recruit through community health centers and social media. Findings will inform culturally competent substance use prevention programs tailored to TGNB young people.

Keywords: transgender youth, substance use, gender affirmation, minority stress, ecological momentary assessment, mixed methods

=========== 2R01ES215678-01.txt ===========
Heat Stress, Green Space, and Pregnancy Outcomes in Urban Heat Island Communities
University of Washington School of Public Health — PI: Clara M. Woodruff

Urban heat islands heighten the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes including preterm birth and low birthweight. This project will combine satellite-derived land surface temperature data, electronic health records from five metropolitan hospitals, and personal temperature monitoring in a cohort of 2000 pregnant individuals across three U.S. cities (Phoenix, Baltimore, and Seattle). We will examine the dose-response relationship between cumulative heat exposure during gestation and birth outcomes. Additionally, we will evaluate whether neighborhood green space access (parks, tree canopy) buffers these effects. Spatial and causal modeling will disentangle the roles of heat, air pollution, and socioeconomic factors. Policy recommendations for climate adaptation in urban planning will be developed.

Keywords: heat stress, urban heat island, pregnancy outcomes, green space, climate adaptation, preterm birth

=========== 2R01HL205678-01.txt ===========
Environmental Particulate Exposure and Cardiac Autonomic Dysfunction in Latinx Agricultural Workers
University of Michigan Ann Arbor — PI: Luis Miguel Castro

Latinx agricultural workers face disproportionate exposure to particulate matter from soil dust and pesticide aerosols. This project will investigate how chronic exposure to inhalable particles (PM2.5 and PM10-2.5) alters cardiac autonomic function using electrocardiographic monitoring and heart rate variability (HRV) analysis. A cohort of 250 workers from Michigan's agricultural regions will be followed over two harvest seasons with personal exposure monitoring and clinical assessments. We will examine the mediating roles of systemic inflammation and oxidative stress biomarkers. Multilevel modeling will account for socioeconomic and occupational covariates. This work will inform occupational safety policies for vulnerable populations.

Keywords: agricultural workers, particulate matter, cardiac autonomic function, heart rate variability, Latinx health, occupational exposure

=========== 2R01MH145678-01.txt ===========
Neural Circuit Dynamics of Social Reward Processing in Adolescent Depression
University of California, San Francisco — PI: Andrea Vazquez-Mendez

Adolescent depression is associated with altered social reward processing that may predict long-term outcomes. This project will use longitudinal fMRI and behavioral experiments to define the neural circuit signatures underlying social reward anticipation and receipt in adolescents aged 14-18. We will compare depressed youth with healthy controls, focusing on ventral tegmental area-medial prefrontal cortex connectivity. We hypothesize that reduced dopamine-mediated signaling in this circuit correlates with social anhedonia. The study will also examine how pubertal hormonal changes modulate these pathways. Results will identify biomarkers for early intervention strategies.

Keywords: adolescent depression, social reward, fMRI, neural circuits, adolescence, dopamine

=========== 2R01NR019876-01.txt ===========
Community Health Worker Intervention to Reduce Maternal Mortality Among African American Women in Rural South Texas
University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio — PI: Aisha Okafor

African American women in rural South Texas experience maternal mortality rates threefold higher than their white counterparts. This community-engaged study will test a culturally tailored intervention deploying community health workers (CHWs) to provide prenatal and postpartum navigation, stress management, and chronic disease screening. A randomized controlled trial with 300 participants will measure outcomes including blood pressure control, gestational diabetes management, mental health access, and birth complication rates. The intervention leverages relationships with local churches and clinics. Process evaluations will identify barriers and facilitators for dissemination to other rural regions with high disparities.

Keywords: maternal mortality, African American women, community health workers, rural health, health disparities, prenatal care

=========== 2R01NR025678-01.txt ===========
Barriers and Facilitators to Colorectal Cancer Screening Among Somali Refugee Communities in the Midwest
University of Florida — PI: Mohammed Al-Hassan

Somali refugees in the U.S. Midwest have extremely low colorectal cancer screening rates due to language barriers, cultural beliefs, mistrust of healthcare systems, and limited health literacy. This community-based participatory project uses a convergent mixed-methods design to identify key barriers and develop a culturally adapted decision-aid tool. In-depth interviews with 60 community members and healthcare providers will be followed by a pilot trial of an illustrated bilingual educational intervention delivered through community elders. Outcomes include screening uptake, changes in colorectal cancer knowledge, and patient navigation satisfaction. The project is guided by a community advisory board of Somali leaders.

Keywords: colorectal cancer screening, Somali refugees, health literacy, cultural adaptation, community-based participatory research, health disparities

=========== R01AG078420-02.txt ===========
Sleep and circadian misalignment as a driver of glycemic dysregulation in shift workers
Stanford University — PI: Harold Benoit

Shift work affects over 15 million Americans and is a recognized risk factor for cardiovascular disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. The underlying mechanisms are poorly understood, but desynchrony between the central circadian clock and peripheral metabolic tissues likely plays a central role. In this project, we will use a rigorous constant routine and forced desynchrony protocol to examine how night scheduling (simulated 3-day night shift) alters glucose homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, and pancreatic beta-cell function in 150 healthy volunteers aged 40-65. We will also measure circadian phase markers (dim-light melatonin onset) and transcriptomic profiles of peripheral blood mononuclear cells to identify clock-regulated genes associated with glycemic outcomes. Additionally, we will test the hypothesis that a timed bright light intervention during the night shift and melatonin suppression can partially restore circadian alignment and improve postprandial glucose (tolerance) responses. Participants will be randomized to either light intervention or control, and we will record continuous glucose monitoring for 72 hours. Successful completion could yield a scalable, behaviorally anchored intervention to reduce type 2 diabetes risk in shift workers, directly informing occupational health guidelines.

Keywords: shift work, circadian rhythm, glucose metabolism, type 2 diabetes, light therapy

=========== R01AG078912-02.txt ===========
Plasma Proteomic and Metabolomic Biomarkers for Early Detection of Alzheimer's Disease in Diverse Populations
Johns Hopkins University — PI: Marcus Whitfield

Detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD) before symptom onset is critical for intervention. Amyloid and tau PET are costly, limiting their use in diverse and underserved populations. We will profile 1200 plasma proteins and 800 metabolites using high-throughput mass spectrometry in 2,500 participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study, ensuring representation of Black and White adults. We will develop a machine learning model integrating these omics with cognitive trajectories and MRI metrics. We will externally validate a top-performing panel in the Mexican Health and Aging Study. The resulting biomarker panel will be evaluated for accuracy against amyloid PET in a subset. This project will provide a cost-effective, scalable blood test for AD risk stratification, aimed at reducing diagnostic disparities in primary care settings.

Keywords: Alzheimer's disease, plasma biomarkers, proteomics, metabolomics, health disparities

=========== R01AI112233-07.txt ===========
Mechanisms of Heteroresistance to Carbapenems in Klebsiella pneumoniae
Washington University in St. Louis — PI: Sofia Marquez

Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) are a global health threat, with heteroresistance enabling treatment failure despite apparent susceptibility. We will dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying carbapenem heteroresistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae using a combination of population analysis profiles, whole-genome sequencing, and single-cell microfluidics. We will test the hypothesis that subpopulations with increased blaKPC copy number or outer membrane porin alterations arise through stochastic gene amplification. We will characterize the fitness costs and compensatory mutations in these subpopulations. Finally, we will evaluate optimized dosing regimens and combination therapies in a murine thigh infection model to suppress emergence of resistant mutants. Our findings will provide the mechanistic basis for revised susceptibility testing protocols and novel, resistance-proof treatment strategies to mitigate the silent spread of this resistance phenotype.

Keywords: Antimicrobial resistance, Klebsiella pneumoniae, heteroresistance, carbapenems, gene amplification

=========== R01AI145678-03.txt ===========
Countering Vaccine Misinformation with Personalized Narratives in Community Health Settings
Emory University — PI: Samuel Osei

Vaccine hesitancy threatens herd immunity for COVID-19, influenza, and routine childhood immunizations. We will test the effectiveness of personalized narrative-based messaging versus standard didactic information in increasing vaccine uptake. We will recruit 1,200 vaccine-hesitant adults from community health centers in Atlanta and rural Georgia. Participants will be randomized to receive either (1) a story from a peer with similar sociodemographic background describing a personal vaccine experience, (2) a factual messaging brochure from CDC, or (3) usual care. The narratives will be developed using computational linguistics on prior interviews to maximize identification. Outcome is vaccine receipt within 3 months, verified by EHR. We will measure psychological reactance and self-efficacy as mediators. We will also test an adaptive approach where message style matches participant's motivational profile (e.g., autonomy vs. community concern). Findings will inform scalable communication strategies to combat misinformation.

Keywords: Vaccine confidence, misinformation, personal narratives, health communication, randomized controlled trial

Emory University — PI: Priya Raghavan

=========== R01CA215120-07.txt ===========
Targeting STK11-mutant non-small cell lung cancer via metabolic vulnerabilities
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute — PI: Marcus Okafor

STK11 (LKB1) mutations are present in approximately 20% of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) and are associated with aggressive tumor behavior, intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, and poor patient outcomes. Despite this clinical significance, there are no approved targeted therapies for STK11-mutant tumors. Our preliminary data reveal that STK11 loss induces a unique metabolic dependency on the serine/glycine biosynthesis pathway and on mitochondrial complex I. This proposal will test the hypothesis that STK11-mutant tumors can be selectively eliminated by inhibiting PHGDH (phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase) combined with metformin, thereby exploiting synthetic lethality. We will use patient-derived xenografts, isogenic cell lines, and organoid models to evaluate efficacy and identify resistance mechanisms. Furthermore, we will investigate the impact of this combination on the tumor immune microenvironment, aiming to resensitize these cold tumors to immunotherapies. Our project will provide a strong rationale for a first-in-class clinical trial combining PHGDH inhibition with metabolic modulators for this high-need patient population.

Keywords: lung cancer, STK11, metabolism, PHGDH, combination therapy, immunotherapy

=========== R01CA231456-04.txt ===========
Single-Cell Genomic Determinants of Therapy Resistance in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute — PI: Elena Rodriguez

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains the most aggressive subtype, with rapid acquisition of resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. We will apply single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing to serial biopsies from a prospective cohort of 120 TNBC patients to identify dynamic transcriptional and chromatin states associated with residual disease. Our preliminary data reveal a distinct persister cell population expressing a stem-like program and elevated homologous recombination repair activity. We will functionally validate these candidates using CRISPR interference in patient-derived organoids and xenografts. The goal is to define predictive biomarkers of resistance and to nominate new combinatorial therapeutic targets. This work will directly inform precision oncology approaches for high-risk TNBC patients and could lead to clinical assays for early detection of non-response.

Keywords: Triple-negative breast cancer, single-cell genomics, chemotherapy resistance, chromatin remodeling, precision oncology

=========== R01CA256880-04.txt ===========
Aging, tumor microenvironment, and DNA damage response in colorectal cancer disparities
University of Michigan — PI: Rebecca Goldstein

Colorectal cancer (CRC) incidence and mortality vary sharply by race and ethnicity, with Black and Hispanic patients experiencing later-stage diagnosis and shorter survival. Biological differences in tumor-immune interactions may underlie some of this disparity, but studies have rarely integrated genomic, tumor-immune, and host aging data in diverse cohorts. This project will analyze multi-omic data from 1200 treatment-naive CRC tumors, including primary tumors from Black, Hispanic, and non-Hispanic White patients, with extensive clinical follow-up. We will generate whole-exome sequencing (mutational signatures, neoantigen load), RNA sequencing (immune cell deconvolution, senescence signatures), and digital spatial profiling of the tumor microenvironment. We will test the hypothesis that higher tumor mutation burden in minority populations is associated with increased AID/APOBEC mutagenesis and an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and also examine the role of biological age (epigenetic clocks) as a modifier. Additionally, we will create and validate a composite risk score that integrates biological and social determinants (neighborhood deprivation, discrimination) to predict survival and recurrence. The project promises to inform equitable, targeted interventions.

Keywords: colorectal cancer, disparities, tumor microenvironment, aging, multi-omics, APOBEC

=========== R01DK128942-02.txt ===========
Food insecurity, stress, and epigenetic aging in American Indian adults with type 2 diabetes
University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center — PI: Ming Wei Liu

American Indian (AI) communities face a 2-3 times higher prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) than the general US population, with severe complications and earlier mortality. Among the psychosocial drivers, food insecurity remains a pervasive issue, affecting up to 50% of AI households. This project aims to determine whether food insecurity accelerates biological aging via chronic stress pathways, specifically corticotropin-releasing hormone and cortisol dysregulation, leading to worsening glycemic control and diabetic complications. We will follow 500 AI adults with T2D for 3 years, measuring food insecurity quarterly via the USDA Household Food Security Survey, collecting hair cortisol to assess chronic stress, and performing DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks (PhenoAge, GrimAge) at baseline and year 3. We will also use structural equation modeling to test the mediating role of stress and epigenetic aging on the relationship between food insecurity and HbA1c trajectories, glomerular filtration rate decline, and retinopathy progression. Our findings will inform culturally grounded, multi-level interventions incorporating food sovereignty and stress-reduction strategies to break this pathway and reduce diabetes 
... [1137 chars truncated] ...
trajectories while identifying psychosocial risk and protective factors. This evidence is critical for clinical guidelines and legislative debates.

Keywords: Gender-affirming care, transgender adolescents, mental health, suicidality, longitudinal cohort

=========== R01HL145678-05.txt ===========
Deep Learning-Based Cardiac MRI for Early Detection of Myocardial Fibrosis in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
Cleveland Clinic — PI: Anika Sharma

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common genetic heart disease, yet current MRI measures of fibrosis lack sensitivity and are subjective. We will develop a deep learning framework that combines cine MRI, native T1 mapping, and late gadolinium enhancement to automatically segment the myocardium and quantify diffuse and replacement fibrosis with high precision. Our method will be trained on 1,500 HCM cases and validated on an independent cohort of 500 patients. We will assess the association of these novel MRI biomarkers with incident arrhythmias and heart failure hospitalization over 5 years. By providing an automated, reproducible pipeline, we aim to improve risk stratification and enable earlier initiation of anti-fibrotic therapies. This project addresses a critical need for robust imaging biomarkers in HCM management.

Keywords: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac MRI, deep learning, myocardial fibrosis, risk stratification

=========== R01HL149850-05.txt ===========
Diverse ancestry exome sequencing to identify novel loci for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Columbia University Medical Center — PI: Alysia Thompson

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a severe, often fatal disease, and current treatment does not stop progression. Genetic causes explain about 30% of hereditable and 5% of sporadic cases, but the great majority of genetic architecture remains unidentified, especially in non-European populations. We will perform whole-exome sequencing in 5,000 PAH cases and 10,000 controls drawn from multi-ancestry cohorts (African American, Hispanic, Asian, and European American) within the NHLBI-funded PAH Biobank and the Pulmonary Hypertension Association Registry. We will conduct single-variant and gene-based burden tests, assess rare and coding variants, and perform a phenome-wide association study in UK Biobank to explore clinical correlates. We will also investigate top candidate genes using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived endothelial cells and pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells to validate functional impacts on apoptosis, proliferation, and endothelial-mesenchymal transition. Ancestry-specific variants, including HLA alleles and novel genes like TSP1, will be prioritized. Our work aims to reveal novel therapeutic targets and improve risk stratification, reduce health disparities in genomic medicine for PAH, and bridge the gap between genetic findings and patient outcomes.

Keywords: pulmonary hypertension, genetics, diverse ancestry, exome sequencing, biomarkers, health disparities

=========== R01MD013760-04.txt ===========
Community health worker intervention to reduce cardiovascular risk in rural Black men
University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston — PI: Carlos Rivera

Rural Black men experience a disproportionately high burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and have the lowest life expectancy among all race-gender groups in the US. Structural barriers, mistrust in the healthcare system, and underrepresentation in clinical trials contribute to this disparity. Our project will implement and evaluate a culturally tailored, community health worker (CHW)-delivered telehealth intervention aimed at reducing blood pressure and improving CVD risk factor profiles among 400 Black men aged 30-70 in the rural Mississippi Delta and South Texas. We will randomize participants to either a 12-month CHW coaching program (including home blood pressure monitoring, lifestyle counseling, and healthcare navigation) or an enhanced usual care group. Primary outcomes are change in systolic blood pressure and the ABCS (aspirin, blood pressure control, cholesterol management, smoking cessation) composite score at 12 months. We will use a community-based participatory research framework, engage local faith-based organizations and barbershops, and conduct in-depth process evaluations to assess feasibility. We hypothesize a clinically significant 8 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure and meaningful improvements in the ABCS score.

Keywords: health disparities, rural health, community health worker, cardiovascular disease, Black men, blood pressure

=========== R01MD045678-03.txt ===========
Community-Based Participatory Research to Reduce Hypertension Disparities in Rural African American Communities
University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill — PI: Latoya Jackson

Rural African American adults experience disproportionately high hypertension and stroke mortality. This study uses a community-based participatory research framework with 8 rural counties in North Carolina. We will implement a multi-level intervention combining home blood pressure monitoring with peer health coaching, culturally tailored dietary education, and telemedicine consultations with pharmacists. A cluster randomized trial will compare this intervention to enhanced usual care in 600 adults with uncontrolled hypertension. Primary outcome is change in systolic blood pressure at 12 months. We will also assess psychosocial mediators and process outcomes. The intervention is co-designed with faith-based and community organizations to ensure sustainability. Our goal is to generate a replicable model to reduce hypertension disparities in underserved rural populations and inform policy changes for telehealth reimbursement.

Keywords: Hypertension disparities, rural health, African American, community-based participatory research, telehealth

=========== R01MH123456-04.txt ===========
A Technology-Based Intervention to Increase PrEP Uptake and Adherence Among Transgender Women
University of California, San Francisco — PI: Ava Thompson

Transgender women face disproportionate HIV incidence, yet PrEP uptake remains low due to stigma, medical mistrust, and structural barriers. We will develop a mobile health (mHealth) intervention integrating a peer-navigator chat function, automated medication reminders, and adaptive messaging tailored to gender-affirmation events. Co-designed with transgender community advisory boards, the app will address specific concerns about hormone-Prep interactions and discrimination in clinics. We will conduct a 12-month randomized controlled trial with 300 transgender women in the San Francisco Bay Area, comparing the mHealth intervention to standard care navigation. Feasibility and usability will be assessed with mixed methods. Primary outcome is PrEP adherence measured by dried blood spot assays. We will also evaluate sustainability of engagement and changes in sexual risk behaviors. This study will provide a scalable, community-centered digital tool to reduce HIV burden in a high-priority population.

Keywords: Transgender women, PrEP, mHealth, HIV prevention, adherence, sexual minority health

=========== R01MH128990-03.txt ===========
Acceptance and commitment therapy for transgender youth: A randomized trial on mental health
University of Washington — PI: Jonathan Park

Transgender and nonbinary (TGNB) youth experience dramatically higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation compared to their cisgender peers, driven by minority stress and identity-specific stigma. Despite the existence of gender-affirming medical care, mental health treatment that coexists and supports such care is scarce. We propose the first fully powered randomized controlled trial (N=240, ages 14-18) comparing a 12-session, trans-diagnostic Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) program, co-designed with TGNB youth, against non-directive supportive counseling. The intervention focuses on psychological flexibility, minority stress coping (enacted stigma, internalized transphobia), and values-based committed action aligned with gender identity. Outcomes include depression severity (CDRS-R), anxiety (SCARED), and suicidal ideation severity at post-treatment, 6- and 12-month follow-ups. We will also examine the moderating effect of family support and gender-affirming medical interventions. Our hypothesis is that ACT will produce significantly greater reductions in depressive symptoms and suicidality, with sustained benefits. This study addresses a critical gap in accessible, scalable psychosocial care for this vulnerable population.

Keywords: transgender youth, mental health, ACT, minority stress, randomized trial

Racial Discrimination, Biological Aging, and Cognitive Decline in Middle-Aged Black Adults
Meharry Medical College — PI: Imani Nelson

This project examines the hypothesis that experiences of racial discrimination accelerate biological aging, leading to earlier cognitive decline in Black adults. We will leverage data from 1,000 middle-aged Black participants in the Nashville Stress and Health Study, who have detailed measures of lifetime discrimination and coping strategies. We will measure epigenetic clocks (GrimAge, PhenoAge) from stored DNA, telomere length, and inflammatory markers. We will conduct a new wave of cognitive assessments (executive function, episodic memory) and 7T MRI to assess hippocampal volume and white matter integrity. Using structural equation modeling, we will estimate the mediating role of biological aging in the discrimination-cognition pathway, and test whether social support moderates these effects. Results will inform psychosocial and policy interventions to interrupt the detrimental health effects of discrimination and reduce dementia risk in minority populations.

Keywords: Racial discrimination, biological aging, cognitive decline, epigenetic clocks, Black adults

==========
Gender-Affirming Care and Longitudinal Mental Health Outcomes in Transgender and Non-Binary Adolescents
Boston Children's Hospital — PI: Emily Hart

Transgender and non-binary (TGNB) adolescents experience severe depression, anxiety, and suicidality. This prospective observational study will follow 450 TGNB adolescents (ages 12-17) receiving gender-affirming care from a multidisciplinary clinic. We will track mental health outcomes (PHQ-9, GAD-7, suicidal ideation) every 6 months for 3 years, alongside documentation of puberty blockers, gender-affirming hormones, and surgical referral. We will use propensity score matching to compare outcomes with a waitlist control group. We will also measure family support, school victimization, and internalized transphobia to identify moderators. A sub-study will collect salivary cortisol to assess stress physiology. The goal is to quantify the association between receipt of gender-affirming interventions and mental health trajectories while identifying psychosocial risk and protective factors. This evidence is critical for clinical guidelines and legislative debates.

Keywords: Gender-affirming care, transgender adolescents, mental health, suicidality, longitudinal cohort

==========
Innate immune training by soil-transmitted helminths and effects on vaccine responses
Emory University — PI: Priya Raghavan

Soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) infect over one billion people worldwide, and chronic infections are known to shape systemic immune responses, potentially blunting vaccine efficacy. In this project, we investigate the hypothesis that STH-induced innate immune training (epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of monocytes) alters the magnitude and quality of antibody and T-cell responses to routine childhood vaccines. Using a controlled human infection model with Necator americanus (hookworm) followed by yellow fever and typhoid vaccines, we will enroll 150 healthy adults in southern India, where STH exposure is endemic. We will perform longitudinal single-cell sequencing, chromatin accessibility assays (ATAC-seq), and functional metabolomics on circulating monocytes, as well as measure vaccine-specific neutralizing antibodies, T follicular helper cells, and memory B cells. We will also assess whether antihelminthic treatment before vaccination restores optimal immune responses. Results will inform public health strategies for deworming and immunization campaigns globally, especially in regions with high STH burden and suboptimal vaccine protection.

Keywords: helminths, vaccine response, innate immune training, monocytes, India, immunization
